questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: The Sorbonne is one the most well-renowned universities in Europe, notably within the discipline of philosophy where its historical and academic influence cannot be underrated. As such, I saw an Erasmus stay at the university as a rare opportunity to go and immerse myself in a philosophically prestigious environment where I would be able to experience first hand the world famous philosophical tradition, which has shaped so much of wester thought since the enlightenment.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Not too easy. Fortunately I had a friend who had done an exchange semester at La Sorbonne the previous semester. He shared the course descriptions with me and helped me understand the procedures of enrollment which, to me, were not at all easy to comprehend otherwise.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: There were e-mails sent containing information, as well as an information meeting before the start of the semester. Much, however, was left to be guessed at. One thing that made it especially hard to make sure I was on the right track, was that I had to be in touch both with office of international relations, the office at the department of philosophy, as well as other departments in which I took elective courses. A centralization of course-finding at enrollment would, I think, make the whole process much more easy and safe.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I found my accommodation via Le Bon Coin — I believe I was exceptionally lucky to be picked by my landlord. I guess my recommendation would be to not give up hope, and to keep on sending those messages to possible renters, even when you got no reply from many.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Seeing as how I have tried no alternative to this way of living, I have no real basis of comparison. I lived alone in a studio and even though I preferred living this way, I did come to lead quite a secluded life style. I guess then, that I would say to future students, that if they go on to live on their one (that is, without housemates), they should prioritize building some sort of social network — even if this can seem a lot of work.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: One was to find the courses within the course description file for each year of each discipline. These were not easy to come by, but I managed, with some luck, to find them at the university webpage after endless clicking and some help from a friend who had previously been to the Sorbonne.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Not much, to my knowledge. I tried contacting the secretary at the philosophy Department, but she was not interested in helping me and simply referred me to the aforementioned files, without any guidance on how to find them.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I managed, after some emailing back and forth to get exactly the courses I had hoped for. I was, however, uncertain about whether I had really gotten them until long after the semester had started — there was no confirmation of registration or anything the like.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: To not loose hope and to know that everything usually works out in the end. I cannot say how many times I was certain that the administrative part of my stay had been messed up. This was never the case; there is just a really slow flow of information.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The style of teaching is quite different to what I was used to from the University of Copenhagen. At the Sorbonne the teaching is more rigid and conservative than that of many other European universities. Many students transcribe the lectures word-for-word which, to me, exemplifies quite well the lack of independence in the studies. Students seem to be expected to know — or, remember — just what they are taught in class, and not much else. There is, thus, not much energy devoted to developing skills in critical thinking, independent reading of texts, or of free philosophical discussion. On Swiss Erasmus student told me, she felt as if she was back in high school. I should say, in all fairness, that the courses being all in French, a third language to me, also inhibited slightly my ability to participate actively in classes. A higher level of French would have made it possible to shape the teaching experience to the better. The above mentioned shortcomings of the classes seemed however to apply to the local students as well.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Se above.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would recommend to take courses at the SIAL (department of foreign language learning), which offer French courses at an academic level. It is nice to be in a class with other exchange students who are there on the same premise as yourself. Further, the academic requirements are somewhat lower, which can be a very welcome relief from the very demanding courses in philosophy, and, I presume, in the other departments as well.

questions.answer: None

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Rent is generally higher than in Copenhagen. I was lucky to find a small studio at 720€/Month excluding heat an electricity, which was about 60-60€/Month in additional costs. I know of Erasmus students who pay even higher rents.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: I did not participate in any, but there were options on offer to do sports and film clubs etc..

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: There is so much to do in Paris! I especially recommend taking advantage of the many museums and galleries.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Easy! The Parisian life style is much of what makes an exchange stay at la Sorbonne worth while. If you are into great and not too expensive food, wine, coffee and cake, massive bookstores, and museums, it should be easy to get into the rhythm.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: I found that the local students in my classes were very closed and unwelcoming. I spoke to many other exchange students who had the same experience. Luckily it is not too hard to find company, as there a many students from abroad at the university. At bars and restaurants as well, it is easy to chat to people and make connections that way.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
i/ Make connections with other students and people in general. It can be quite lonely going to the Sorbonne, and even if it seems that you do not have the time to socialize because the workload from the university is to great — I would say it pays off to take that time.

ii/ Practice your French as much as possible. Many people think that if they can just achieve a B2 level which is the admission requirements, they will be all right. This is true to some extend, but you will safe yourself so much headache by really practicing hard — preferably with a tandem partner in Copenhagen. The better your French the better your whole experience!

iii/ Build knowledge of the specific academic writing genres, 'la dissertation', 'l'explication d'un texte,' and 'le commentaire composé'. These are not intuitive and require to be studied before you can complete the exams.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: It was very rewarding to actually complete what at times seemed an insurmountable challenge. I really struggled during my semester, so it was nice to be able to complete it. I was proud of that, and happy to see my level of French greatly improved — especially in writing and reading.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Definitely getting in to the French academic tradition, which is quite different to the Danish. To be honest, I found that it was more demanding, but somehow still less rewarding. I am happy to have acquired a level of French that permits me to now work with French texts in my further studies, but the actual academic outcome from the courses was not very giving, and thus a challenge to keep following.

questions.answer: Yes
